agriculture_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: The largest source of emissions in Austrian agriculture is enteric fermentation in cattle, which releases methane (CH₄). The overall cattle population is therefore the most important driver of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.
note.p2: The other large sources are the management of organic fertilizer (manure and slurry) and the nitrogen fertilization of agricultural soils. Both release nitrous oxide (N₂O), whose global warming potential is 265 (IPCC 2013).
note.p3: Energy-related emissions within the sector, from mobile machinery and stationary combustion, are also attributed to agriculture.

buildings_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: Emissions from the Austrian buildings sector come mostly from natural gas and heating oil burned for space and domestic water heating. Both private household buildings and commercial buildings are included.
note.p2: The two largest shares of the sector's energy use are, however, biomass and electricity — visible in the energy use charts further down.

emissions_fuels_yearly.title: AT CO2 emissions by fuels: yearly (incl. projection)

note.p1: Official, detailed emission statistics only appear several months after the year they describe. Timely fossil fuel consumption data still allows a rough projection, shown on the left with its uncertainty bars; the method is written up in full under {methodology}.
note.p2: In short: the fossil fuel consumption eurostat reports is extrapolated to the full year and converted through emission factors into energy-sector emissions (transport, buildings, energy & industry, process emissions included). The remaining sectors — agriculture, waste, fluorinated gases — are carried forward along their current trend.
note.p3: The model is deliberately simple and rests on past data and temporal correlation. Extrapolated values must therefore be read with great care, especially early in the year.
note.p4: Estimated monthly and yearly emissions for every fuel considered are shown below. Consumption of the individual fuels is on the {fossil_fuels} page.

energy_industry_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: CO₂ emissions in the energy and industry sector come from a range of sub-sectors, and process emissions have to be told apart from energy-related ones. Energy-related emissions come from burning fossil fuels to produce power or heat; process emissions are a by-product of industrial production and do not necessarily rest on fossil fuels at all — cement production is the classic case.
note.p2: The largest absolute contributions are electricity and district heat generation (mainly natural gas), process and energy emissions in iron and steel (coal and natural gas), energy-related emissions of other industries such as pulp and paper (natural gas and oil), refineries (oil), and process emissions in the chemical industry (natural gas for ammonia production) and the mineral industry (cement and lime).

fluorinated_gases_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: Fluorinated gases are a group of fluorine-containing molecules (SF₆, NF₃, PFCs, HFCs) used across a range of industries and products.
note.p2: The main driver today is hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) as refrigerants in refrigeration and stationary air conditioning. They were adopted widely from 1993 to replace the ozone-depleting HCFCs; their use is now restricted in the EU and emissions have begun to fall.
note.p3: The rest comes from mobile air conditioning in cars, also declining under EU restrictions, and from a range of smaller uses grouped under “Other” — foam blowing agents, and SF₆ insulation in particle accelerators and high-voltage electrical equipment.

long_term_storage_c_disposal.title: AT long-term storage of C in waste disposal sites

note.p1: LULUCF is short for Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry. The sector covers every greenhouse gas emission tied to how land in Austria is used, and to changes between land use types.
note.p2: As the chart shows, the sector can act as a substantial emission sink, because it also accounts for the CO₂ bound in forests, in soil and in land mass generally. When land use changes — grassland or forest turned into settlement, say — emissions arise from the different amounts of carbon the two types can store.
note.p3: Forest land has always been the largest contributor and dictates the trend of the sector as a whole. Growing forest mass made LULUCF a net sink in Austria for decades; that trend has weakened in recent years, and individual years with net positive emissions have occurred.

transport_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: Transport emissions, as accounted for under the international reporting standards, come almost entirely from burning gasoline and diesel on the road — passenger cars and duty vehicles. Shipping, rail, domestic aviation and mobile military vehicles contribute little and are grouped under “Other”.
note.p2: International aviation is not part of the national emission statistics, although the kerosene burned for it contributes substantially in reality — see the kerosene consumption chart further down.
note.p3: The data on this page is mostly road transport: monthly fuel consumption, and new registrations and stock of the vehicle classes by type of motor energy.

waste_emissions_sectors.info: Scaled to UBA totals, later years carried forward.

note.p1: Waste sector emissions have historically been dominated by methane (CH₄) from biological waste in landfills. Stricter legislation and policy measures have cut the amount of untreated waste going to landfill considerably.
note.p2: Today most of the sector's emissions come from incinerating waste in power plants to produce electricity and heat. The net CO₂ here comes from the non-biogenic fraction — plastics and industrial waste.
note.p3: Smaller fractions are CH₄ and N₂O from biological waste treatment (composting) and from waste water treatment in sewage plants.
